pos: n. (proper name; the plain in Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden image)
etymology: Aramaic Dura', circle or walled enclosure, a common Mesopotamian place-name element.
biblical_def: Dura is the plain where Nebuchadnezzar raised his idol: “Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits: he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon” (Daniel 3:1). Every officer of the empire was summoned to its dedication, and the herald proclaimed that at the sound of the music all must fall down and worship, and “whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace” (Daniel 3:6). On that plain three young Jews remained standing. Their answer is the charter of faithful refusal: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Daniel 3:17-18). Dura is the field where the state demanded worship and found that the servants of the Most High would give it obedience in everything except that.

corruption_summary: Civil religion asks for a token bow and calls refusal extremism; the three on the plain of Dura answered that worship belongs to God alone.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age has its plain of Dura: a demand from the state or the culture for a gesture of allegiance that belongs only to God. The demand is always presented as small and reasonable, and refusal as fanaticism.

The principle to recover is the limit of civil authority. The three Hebrews were loyal servants of Babylon in all lawful things; they would not bow to its image. We ought to obey God rather than men, whether God delivers from the furnace or not.

pos: n. (proper name; a Syrian land under the burden of the LORD in Zechariah 9)
etymology: Hebrew Chadrak, a foreign name, the Hatarikka of Assyrian records, a district near Hamath.
biblical_def: Hadrach opens one of the great oracles of Zechariah: “The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof: when the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel, shall be toward the LORD” (Zechariah 9:1). The burden moves south through Syria and the coast, “And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise” (Zechariah 9:2), and on to the cities of the Philistines. Hadrach was long unknown outside this verse, until Assyrian records yielded Hatarikka, a district near Hamath. The oracle sweeps over the nations that had troubled Israel, and then turns, in the same chapter, to Zion's King: “behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass” (Zechariah 9:9). The judgment that begins in Hadrach clears the way for the coming of Christ.

pos: n. (proper name; the city named for Gog's multitude in Ezekiel 39)
biblical_def: Hamonah is the name Ezekiel gives to a city near the burial place of Gog's armies: “And also the name of the city shall be Hamonah. Thus shall they cleanse the land” (Ezekiel 39:16). The context is the end of the Gog prophecy. After the LORD destroys the hosts that come against His people, He gives Gog “a place there of graves in Israel, the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea”, and “they shall call it The valley of Hamongog” (Ezekiel 39:11), the valley of Gog's multitude. The burying takes seven months, and men are appointed to search the land so that not a bone is left to defile it. Hamonah, the multitude, is the town that will stand as a memorial of the multitude that fell. The point of the prophecy is the holiness of the land and of the God who cleanses it: the enemy's greatness becomes only a name over a graveyard.

The principle to recover is that every enemy of God's people ends in His judgment and every defilement ends in His cleansing. Hamonah is a memorial: the multitude that came against Israel is remembered only by its grave.

pos: n. (proper name; an Egyptian city where Judah's ambassadors sought help)
etymology: Hebrew Chanes, from Egyptian, probably Heracleopolis (Egyptian Hnes) in Middle Egypt.
biblical_def: Hanes is named in Isaiah's woe against Judah's embassy to Egypt: “For his princes were at Zoan, and his ambassadors came to Hanes” (Isaiah 30:4). The chapter opens, “Woe to the rebellious children, saith the LORD, that take counsel, but not of me” (Isaiah 30:1), and names the sin: they “walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh” (Isaiah 30:2). Judah's envoys went deep into Egypt, to Zoan in the delta and Hanes far up the Nile, carrying treasure on asses and camels through the wilderness to buy an alliance against Assyria. The LORD answered, “Therefore shall the strength of Pharaoh be your shame” (Isaiah 30:3). Hanes is the end of that long road of unbelief. The same chapter offers the alternative Judah refused: “In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not” (Isaiah 30:15).

The principle to recover is that the people of God must not make flesh their arm. The world's strength becomes the believer's shame when it is trusted in place of the LORD.

pos: n. (proper name; the region east of Jordan on the border of Ezekiel's restored land)
etymology: Hebrew Chavran, perhaps cave-land or hollow, from chor, cave, hole.
biblical_def: Hauran is the region east of the Sea of Galilee and north of Gilead, named twice in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land. The northern border runs to “Hazarhatticon, which is by the coast of Hauran” (Ezekiel 47:16), and the eastern border is measured “from Hauran, and from Damascus, and from Gilead, and from the land of Israel by Jordan, from the border unto the east sea” (Ezekiel 47:18). The Hauran was volcanic, fertile and rich in caves, which may explain its name; in later history it was the heart of the province the Greeks called Auranitis. Ezekiel's borders, drawn “according to the twelve tribes of Israel” (Ezekiel 47:13), belong to the vision that begins with the river flowing from the temple and healing the Dead Sea. The border by Hauran frames a land renewed, in a vision whose fulfilment the New Testament finds in Christ and in the city where the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb.

pos: n. (proper name or title; she who is led captive in Nahum's fall of Nineveh)
etymology: Hebrew Hutstsab, it is decreed or she is established, from natsab, to set up, to station; whether a name, a title of the queen, or a verb is disputed.
biblical_def: Huzzab appears once, in Nahum's vision of the fall of Nineveh: “And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts” (Nahum 2:7). The King James translators took the word as a name, perhaps of Nineveh's queen or of the city personified as a woman; their margin offers “that which was established”, and many readers have taken it as a verb, it is decreed. Either way the picture is the same: the proud mistress of Assyria carried off, her women moaning like doves and beating their breasts. Nineveh had been “of old like a pool of water”, and now “they shall flee away. Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back” (Nahum 2:8). The empire that carried Israel captive is itself led captive. Nahum's book is “The burden of Nineveh” (Nahum 1:1), and Huzzab is the burden's human face.

corruption_paragraphs: Nahum is often treated as an embarrassing celebration of an enemy's ruin. Its opening chapter grounds everything in the character of God: slow to anger and great in power, who will not at all acquit the wicked, and a stronghold to them that trust Him.

The principle to recover is that God's justice is good news for the oppressed. Assyria had led nations captive; Huzzab led captive is the answer of heaven to the cry of the nations Assyria had crushed.

pos: n. (proper name; the place north of Damascus to which Abram pursued the kings)
biblical_def: Hobah is the farthest point of Abram's pursuit of the four kings who had carried off Lot: “And he divided himself against them, he and his servants, by night, and smote them, and pursued them unto Hobah, which is on the left hand of Damascus” (Genesis 14:15). On the left hand, to one facing east as the Hebrews oriented themselves, means north. Abram had armed “his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen” and chased the victors of the Vale of Siddim from Dan to beyond Damascus. “And he brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot” (Genesis 14:16). The victory was not Abram's glory but God's, as Melchizedek said on his return: “blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand” (Genesis 14:20). Hobah, the hiding place, is where the fleeing kings found none. The man of faith who would not take a thread from Sodom had pursued them to the edge of the known world for a kinsman.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Gomer, Hosea's wife)
etymology: Hebrew Diblayim, two cakes of figs, dual of debelah, a pressed cake of figs.
biblical_def: Diblaim is named once, as the father of the prophet Hosea's wife: “So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; which conceived, and bare him a son” (Hosea 1:3). The command that sent Hosea to her is one of the hardest in Scripture: “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD” (Hosea 1:2). Gomer became the living parable of Israel, a wife who went after other lovers and whom her husband was commanded to love again, “according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine” (Hosea 3:1). Diblaim's name, a pair of fig-cakes, has been read by some as a hint of Gomer's price or as simply a family name; nothing is certain. His single mention roots the parable in a real household. Hosea did not marry a symbol; he married the daughter of a named man in Israel.

corruption_paragraphs: Interpreters uneasy with God's command to Hosea have often made the marriage a vision or a literary device. Naming Gomer's father anchors it in history, and the force of the prophecy depends on its reality: God's love for faithless Israel was as costly as Hosea's for Gomer.

The principle to recover is the covenant love of God for an unfaithful people. I will betroth thee unto me for ever, the LORD says through Hosea, and the gospel is that promise kept in Christ, who loved His church while she was yet in her sins.

pos: n. (proper name; a chamberlain of Ahasuerus who pointed to Haman's gallows; also Harbonah)
etymology: Persian, perhaps ass-driver or bald; the meaning is uncertain. Esther 7:9 spells it Harbonah.
biblical_def: Harbona is one of the seven chamberlains of king Ahasuerus. He first appears among those sent to fetch queen Vashti: “he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10). He appears again at the turning point of the book, spelled Harbonah. When Esther had exposed Haman at her banquet and the king had gone out in wrath, “Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon” (Esther 7:9). “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 7:10). God is not named in Esther, but His providence is everywhere in it, and one of its instruments is a court servant who knew where the gallows stood and spoke at the moment it mattered.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of providence. God governs all His creatures and all their actions, so that a servant's word and a king's sleepless night serve His purpose for His people. The wicked falls into the ditch which he made.

pos: n. (proper name; grandfather of king Amon of Judah, of Jotbah)
etymology: Hebrew Charuts, diligent or sharp, from charats, to cut, to decide, also the word for gold and for diligence.
biblical_def: Haruz is named once, as the father of a queen-mother: “Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah” (2 Kings 21:19). Kings regularly names the mother of each king of Judah, because the queen-mother held real influence at court. Haruz's daughter married Manasseh, the most wicked of Judah's kings, and her son Amon followed his father: “he walked in all the way that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshipped them” (2 Kings 21:21). Manasseh repented in his old age; Amon did not, and his servants slew him in his own house after two years. Haruz's town, Jotbah, may have lain in Galilee, which would make Amon's mother a northerner brought into the house of David. His name, diligent, sits beside a grandson remembered only for diligence in evil.

corruption_summary: Children are thought to start free of their parents' patterns; Amon walked in all the way his father walked, and did not share his father's late repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern optimism expects each generation to begin anew. Amon learned his father's idolatry thoroughly and missed his father's repentance entirely, which is the danger of a late conversion in a household already formed by sin.
The principle to recover is the weight of parental example. Fathers and mothers who walk in sin teach it, and grace that comes late to a parent may come too late for a child's formation.
